As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time where a Democrat and a candidate from both major parties won all three of Delaware's counties in a gubernatorial election. ==General election== Democrat and Republican candidates were unopposed in their party primaries, which were held on September 11. '''Gregg''': {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Mitch Daniels]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Mike Pence]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | map_alt = Indiana Governor Election Results by County, 2012 }} {{ElectionsIN}} {{Mike Pence series}} The '''2012 Indiana gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2012. Incumbent [[Governor of Indiana|governor]] [[Mitch Daniels]] was term-limited and unable to seek a third term. The Republican candidate, Congressman [[Mike Pence]]; the Democratic candidate, former [[Speaker of the Indiana House of Representatives]] [[John R. Gregg]]; and the Libertarian candidate, youth mentor, small business owner and reality TV personality, [[Rupert Boneham]], were all unopposed in their respective primaries or conventions, and contested the general election. This is the first open Indiana gubernatorial election since [[1996 Indiana gubernatorial election|1996]] and the first gubernatorial election since [[1972 Indiana gubernatorial election|1972]] without the incumbent governor or [[Lieutenant Governor of Indiana|lieutenant governor]] as a nominee. When the polls closed, the election was very close, and continued to stay close throughout the night. Gregg performed well in [[Marion County, Indiana|Marion County]] (Indianapolis) and [[Lake County, Indiana|Lake County]] (Gary), which were Democratic strongholds. Pence performed well in the [[Indianapolis]] suburbs and the [[Fort Wayne]] area. At 12:34 am EST, the [[Associated Press]] called the race for Pence. At 1:06 am, Gregg called Pence to concede, realizing there were not enough votes left to overtake him. Pence ultimately won the election and took office on January 14, 2013. This was the closest race for governor since [[1960 Indiana gubernatorial election|1960]]. ==Primaries== ===Democratic=== * [[John R. '''Spence''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = [[Governor of Missouri|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jay Nixon]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jay Nixon]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsMO}} The '''2012 Missouri gubernatorial election''' was held on November 6, 2012, to elect the [[List of Governors of Missouri|Governor]] of [[Missouri]]. Incumbent Democratic Governor [[Jay Nixon]] won re-election against the Republican nominee, businessman [[Dave Spence]], despite incumbent President [[Barack Obama]] [[2012 United States presidential election in Missouri|losing Missouri on the same day]] to Republican nominee [[Mitt Romney]]. {{As of|2025}}, this is the last time a Democrat won the governorship of Missouri and the last time that a governor and lieutenant governor of different political parties were simultaneously elected in Missouri. Even with President [[Barack Obama]] losing the state by a nine-point margin, Nixon and Senator [[Claire McCaskill]] both won reelection easily. Like his Senatorial colleague, Nixon was able to get a huge number of votes from rural areas. Both Nixon and McCaskill were declared the winners of their respective races even before the known Democratic strongholds of [[St. Louis]] and [[Kansas City]] came in. {{Election box begin | Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Brian Schweitzer]] was term-limited and could not run for re-election to a third term. [[Montana Department of Justice|Montana Attorney General]] [[Steve Bullock (American politician)|Steve Bullock]] won the Democratic primary with 87% of the vote, and former U.S. Representative [[Rick Hill]] won the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] primary with 34% of the vote. In the general election, Bullock won by 7,571 votes, taking 48.9% of the vote to Hill's 47.3%.Michael Barone, et al. ''The Almanac of American Politics 2014'' (2013) (Kindle Locations 48242-48245). With a margin of 1.6%, this election was the second-closest race of the [[2012 United States gubernatorial elections|2012 gubernatorial election cycle]], behind only [[2012 Puerto Rico gubernatorial election|the election in Puerto Rico]]. Due to the close margin, media outlets did not call the race for Bullock until the next day.{{Cite web|url=https://mtstandard.com/news/state-and-regional/networks-declare-bullock-winner-in-tight-race-for-governor/article_612a52fb-6e9e-59a0-9707-a99cba364cfd.html|title=Networks declare Bullock winner in tight race for governor|author=Charles S. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Bev Perdue]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Pat McCrory]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in North Carolina sidebar}} The '''2012 North Carolina gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2012, concurrently with the [[2012 United States presidential election in North Carolina|2012 United States presidential election]], [[2012 United States House of Representatives elections in North Carolina|U.S. House election]], [[2012 North Carolina judicial election|statewide judicial election]], [[2012 North Carolina Council of State election|Council of State election]], and various local elections. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Governor of North Carolina|Governor]] [[Bev Perdue]] was eligible to run for re-election, but announced on January 26, 2012 that she would not seek a second term. Incumbent lieutenant governor [[Walter Dalton]] won the Democratic nomination, while former mayor of Charlotte and [[2008 North Carolina gubernatorial election|2008 gubernatorial nominee]] [[Pat McCrory]] won the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nomination. McCrory won the election with almost 55 percent of the vote to Dalton's 43 percent, the largest margin of victory for a Republican in a race for governor in history, surpassing the previous record set in [[1868 North Carolina gubernatorial election|1868]]. McCory also outperformed (by 9.35%) Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney’s victory margin in the concurrent presidential race. [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] nominee Barbara Howe took 2% of the vote. When McCrory was inaugurated as the 74th governor of North Carolina on January 5, 2013,{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.pbs.org/video/nc-now-governor-pat-mccrory-swearing-ceremony/ |title=NC Now {{!}} Governor Pat McCrory Swearing In Ceremony {{!}} Season 2013 {{!}} Episode 3004 |language=en |access-date=2025-06-27 |via=www.pbs.org}} he became the state's first Republican governor since 1993 and the Republicans held complete control of state government for the first time since 1871. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time a Republican was elected governor of North Carolina, and the only time since [[1988 North Carolina gubernatorial election|1988]]. It was also the last time the state concurrently voted for a gubernatorial and presidential candidate of the same party, and the last time a Republican candidate won [[Mecklenburg County, North Carolina|Mecklenburg County]] in a statewide election. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== * Bruce Blackmon, physician[http://projects.newsobserver.com/under_the_dome/90year_old_physician_files_in_democratic_primary_for_governor News & Observer: 90-year-old physician files in Democratic primary] * [[Walter Dalton]], lieutenant governor[http://projects.newsobserver.com/under_the_dome/dalton_makes_it_official_he_will_seek_governors_office Dalton makes it official: He will seek governor's office | newsobserver.com projects] * Gary M. align=center| — | {{party shading/Undecided}} align=center| '''39%''' |} ===Debates=== A series of televised debates between candidates Dalton, Etheridge and Faison, held April 16–18, was considered potentially pivotal, since "the governor’s race has so far attracted little attention, created little buzz and produced few political commercials" and "polls suggest there is still a large swath of Democratic voters who have yet to decide" for whom to vote.[http://www.newsobserver.com/2012/04/16/2004259/debate-athon-democratic-gubernatorial.html News & Observer: Democratic gubernatorial candidates' hopes ride on three nights of debate] The first debate, conducted by [[WRAL-TV]] and broadcast statewide, featured few differences between the candidates, but Faison was seen as the aggressor.[http://www.newsobserver.com/2012/04/17/2006172/little-discord-at-north-carolina.html News & Observer: Little discord at NC Democratic gubernatorial debate] The second debate (conducted by [[UNC-TV]]) was more contentious, with Dalton criticizing Etheridge's support of a [[free trade agreement]] while he was in Congress, and Etheridge attacking Dalton over his attendance record on boards and commissions and his alleged failure to speak out against the actions of the majority-Republican legislature.[http://www.newsobserver.com/2012/04/17/2008344/democratic-gubernatorial-debate.html News & Observer: Democratic gubernatorial debate: Criticism grows sharper] In the final debate of the series, this one conducted by [[WNCN-TV]] and the North Carolina [[League of Women Voters]], candidates were considered to be more "muted" in their criticisms of each other. All three spoke out strongly against a [[Voter ID laws|voter ID]] bill proposed by Republicans in the state legislature. Dalton emphasized modernizing the state's economy, Etheridge continued his themes of leadership and education, and Faison most sharply attacked Republicans and called for action on the state's unemployment problem.[http://www.newsobserver.com/2012/04/18/2010404/candidates-vow-to-veto-voter-id.html News & Observer: Democratic candidates vow to veto voter ID bills] ===Results=== [[File:2012 [[C-SPAN]] Dalton and McCrory met for their first televised debate at the studios of [[UNC-TV]] on October 3, 2012. Two debates were sponsored by the North Carolina Association of Broadcasters Educational Foundation, with the third and final debate sponsored by [[WRAL-TV]] and the [[Rocky Mount, North Carolina|Rocky Mount]] Chamber of Commerce. Howe was not invited to participate in any of the scheduled debates. The Associated Press characterized Dalton as going "on the offensive" against McCrory in the first debate.[http://www.newsobserver.com/2012/10/03/2387121/ncs-major-party-gubernatorial.html Associated Press/News & Observer] The final encounter between the two candidates, held Oct. 24 on the campus of [[North Carolina Wesleyan College]], featured "more subdued disagreements over taxes, education, health care and mental health."[http://www.newsobserver.com/2012/10/24/2436595/a-few-jabs-but-no-knockout-in.html News & Observer] ===Polling=== {| class="wikitable" |- valign= bottom ! 2012 North Dakota gubernatorial election.text:

'''Dalrymple''': {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}}
'''Taylor''': {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Jack Dalrymple]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jack Dalrymple]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | image2 = File:Ryan Taylor, 15 September 2012 (cropped).png | nominee2 = [[Ryan Taylor (politician)|Ryan Taylor]] | party2 = North Dakota Democratic–Nonpartisan League Party | running_mate2 = Ellen Chaffee | popular_vote2 = 109,048 | percentage2 = 34.31% }} {{ElectionsND}} The '''2012 North Dakota gubernatorial election''' was held on November 6, 2012, to elect a [[Governor of North Dakota|governor]] and [[lieutenant governor of North Dakota]], concurrently with the [[2012 United States presidential election|2012 U.S. presidential election]], [[2012 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]], [[2012 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2012 North Dakota elections|state and local elections]]. Incumbent Governor [[Jack Dalrymple]] succeeded to the office when then-Governor [[John Hoeven]] resigned to take a seat in the U.S. Senate in [[2010 United States Senate election in North Dakota|2010]]. Dalrymple, a member of the [[North Dakota Republican Party|Republican Party]], won election to a full term. [[Ryan Taylor (politician)|Ryan Taylor]] was the [[North Dakota Democratic-Nonpartisan League Party|Democratic]] nominee. Dalrymple prevailed with 63% of the vote; he declined to seek re-election in 2016. ==Republican Party== ===Candidates=== The [[North Dakota Republican Party]] selected incumbent [[Governor of North Dakota|Governor]] [[Jack Dalrymple]] as their nominee. Incumbent [[Lieutenant Governor of North Dakota|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Drew Wrigley]] was his running mate. Dalrymple defeated Fargo architect Paul Sorum, who later ran as an independent. ====Declined==== * [[Ed Schafer]], former [[governor of North Dakota]] and former [[United States Secretary of Agriculture|U.S. secretary of agriculture]]{{cite web|url=http://www.inforum.com/event/article/id/318497/group/News/|title=Schafer says he's not interested in run for governor|date=May 5, 2011|access-date=May 9, 2011|work=[[The Forum of Fargo-Moorhead]]|first=Terri|last=Finneman}} ==Libertarian Party== ===Candidates=== The [[Libertarian Party of North Dakota]] selected [[Roland Riemers]], a real estate investor, failed 2010 candidate for Grand Forks County sheriff, and failed 1996 candidate for president, as their candidate.{{cite news|last=Smith|first=Nick|title=Roland Riemers enters governor's race|url=http://bismarcktribune.com/news/local/govt-and-politics/roland-riemers-enters-governor-s-race/article_e0aeb3e0-8e42-11e1-9aa0-0019bb2963f4.html|access-date=May 18, 2012|newspaper=[[The Bismarck Tribune]]|date=April 24, 2012}} On July 5, 2012, it was announced that Riemers would not appear on the ballot because his running mate, Richard Ames, failed to file a page of his paperwork.[http://www.grandforksherald.com/event/article/id/240129/group/homepage/] {{dead link|date=January 2018}} On September 12, 2012, after being disqualified from appearing on the ballot, Riemers, a Libertarian now running as an independent with Anthony Johns, said in a news release that he had submitted more than 1,100 signatures to the secretary of state. The pair appeared on the ballot certified by the secretary on Monday.[http://www.thedickinsonpress.com/event/article/id/61267/] {{dead link|date=January 2018}} Riemers filed a lawsuit to have the other candidates removed from the ballot.{{cite web|url=https://secure.forumcomm.com/?publisher_ID=40&article_id=247576&CFID=587988136&CFTOKEN=43514366|title=- Grand Forks Herald - Grand Forks, North Dakota|website=Secure.forumcomm.com|access-date=5 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084910/https://secure.forumcomm.com/?publisher_ID=40&article_id=247576&CFID=587988136&CFTOKEN=43514366|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}{{cite web|url=http://www.ndcourts.gov/court/calendar/20120353.htm|title=Riemers v. Four-term incumbent governor [[John Lynch (New Hampshire governor)|John Lynch]] was eligible to seek a fifth term. In the fall of 2011, Lynch announced that he would retire rather than run for re-election.{{cite web|url=http://www.concordmonitor.com/article/280220/lynch-will-not-seek-fifth-term?SESS9482bdb3cd2a8e91e34f157844e8e08|title=Lynch will not seek a fifth term|date=September 16, 2011|access-date=May 20, 2012|work=[[Concord Monitor]]|first=Karen|last=Langley}}{{Dead link|date=August 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }} On September 11, 2012, Democrat [[Maggie Hassan]] and Republican [[Ovide Lamontagne]] defeated primary opponents to win their parties' nominations.{{cite web|url=http://sos.nh.gov/2012ElectionInfo.aspx|title=2012 Election Information|access-date=May 20, 2012|work=New Hampshire Secretary of State}}{{cite web|url=http://www.unionleader.com/article/20120911/NEWS06/120919916|title=Lamontagne, Hassan will face off in governor's race|access-date=September 11, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129054644/http://www.unionleader.com/article/20120911/NEWS06/120919916|archive-date=November 29, 2014|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} Hassan won the election while carrying every county in the state and began the two-year term on January 3, 2013.[http://elections.nytimes.com/2012/results/states/new-hampshire New Hampshire] ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== * [[Jackie Cilley]], former state Senator{{cite web|url=http://www.unionleader.com/article/20120207/NEWS06/702089988|title=Former state Sen. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Peter Shumlin]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Peter Shumlin]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsVT}} The '''2012 Vermont gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2012, to elect the [[Governor of Vermont|Governor]] of [[Vermont]]. Incumbent Democratic Governor [[Peter Shumlin]] won re-election to a second term, making this the only one of his gubernatorial elections in which he won a majority of the vote. In his [[2010 Vermont gubernatorial election|2010]] and [[2014 Vermont gubernatorial election|2014]] races, the [[Vermont General Assembly]] was required to choose a winner in accordance with the state constitution, because no candidate won a majority. This is the last time that Democrats carried Grand Isle, Lamoille, and Rutland counties in a gubernatorial election. ==Democratic nomination== ===Candidates=== * [[Peter Shumlin]], incumbent{{cite '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Christine Gregoire]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jay Inslee]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Washington State}} The '''2012 Washington gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2012.{{cite web|title=Washington's 2012 elections|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_gubernatorial_election,_2012|website=ballotpedia - The Encyclopedia of American Politics|publisher=ballotpedia|access-date=28 June 2017|archive-date=8 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170508205934/https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_gubernatorial_election,_2012|url-status=live}} Candidates in the election were chosen in an August 7, 2012{{Cite web|url=http://apps.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=29a.04.311|title=RCW 29a.04.311: Primaries.|website=apps.leg.wa.gov|access-date=2011-07-02|archive-date=2011-08-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110813074429/http://apps.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=29A.04.311|url-status=live}} primary election, under the state's [[nonpartisan blanket primary]] system, which allows voters to vote for any candidate running in the race, regardless of party affiliation. The two candidates who received the most votes in the primary election qualified for the general election.[http://wei.secstate.wa.gov/osos/en/Pages/Top2PrimaryFAQ.aspx Pages - Top 2 Primary] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110425233538/http://wei.secstate.wa.gov/osos/en/Pages/Top2PrimaryFAQ.aspx |date=April 25, 2011 }} Incumbent Governor [[Christine Gregoire]] decided to retire rather than seek a third term.{{cite news|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/2-terms-and-out-for-gov-chris-gregoire/|title=2 terms and out for Gov. Chris Gregoire|date=June 13, 2011|access-date=June 13, 2011|work=[[The Seattle Times]]|first=Andrew|last=Garber|archive-date=June 16, 2011|url-access=limited|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110616090459/http://seattletimes.nwsource.com/html/localnews/2015308479_gregoire14m.html|url-status=live}} She endorsed fellow Democrat Jay Inslee, a U.S. Congressman, as her successor. On March 20, 2012, Inslee resigned from Congress in order to focus on his gubernatorial campaign.{{cite news|last=Grygiel|first=Chris|title=US Rep. Inslee to resign for Wash. gov. race|url=http://www.thenewstribune.com/2012/03/10/2061446/ap-sources-wash-rep-inslee-to.html|newspaper=The News Tribune|date=March 10, 2012|agency=Associated Press}}{{Dead link|date=December 2015}} Inslee and Republican [[Rob McKenna]], the [[Attorney General of Washington]], advanced to the general election. 2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial election.title: 2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial recall election
2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial election.text:
{{Short description|Recall election in US state}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2012}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial recall election | country = Wisconsin | type = presidential | ongoing = No | previous_election = 2010 Wisconsin gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2010 | next_election = 2014 Wisconsin gubernatorial election | next_year = 2014 | election_date = June 5, 2012 | image1 = Barrett Walker debate (7314504544) (2).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]]''' | party1 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = '''1,335,585''' | percentage1 = '''53.08%''' | image2 = File:Independence Day 2014 (14418050490) (Tom Barrett) (1).jpg | nominee2 = [[Tom Barrett (Wisconsin politician)|Tom Barrett]] | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 1,164,480 | percentage2 = 46.28% | turnout = 57.8% ({{increase}} 8.1%) | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial recall election results map by county.svg|260px]] |County results |[[File:2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial recall election results map by congressional district.svg|260px]] |Congressional district results |[[File:2012 Wisconsin Gubernatorial election by Precinct.svg|260px]] |Precinct results |default=1}} | map_caption = '''Walker:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} {{legend0|#A80000|>90%}}
'''Barrett:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} {{legend0|#0D0596|>90%}}
'''Tie''': {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsWI}} The '''2012 Wisconsin gubernatorial recall election''' was an [[election]] to elect the [[Governor of Wisconsin|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Wisconsin|lieutenant governor of Wisconsin]]. It resulted in voters re-electing incumbent Republican governor [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]] over the Democratic candidate [[Tom Barrett (Wisconsin politician)|Tom Barrett]] by a larger margin than in [[Wisconsin gubernatorial election, 2010|2010]] when Walker also faced Barrett. Recall organizers opposed Walker's agenda, particularly his limiting of collective bargaining rights for state employees,{{cite news|url=http://archive.boston.com/news/politics/articles/2012/06/04/wisconsin_recall_battle_finally_goes_to_voters/|title=Wisconsin recall battle finally goes to voters|author=Scott Bauer|newspaper=Boston Globe|agency=Associated Press|date=June 4, 2012|access-date=June 4, 2012}} and they collected over 900,000 signatures to initiate the recall election process. There was also a recall for Lieutenant Governor [[Rebecca Kleefisch]]. She won her race, defeating Democrat Mahlon Mitchell, making her the first lieutenant governor to run in and survive a recall.{{cite web|url=http://www.news8000.com/news/Wisconsin-Lieutenant-Governor-Kleefisch-survives-recall-election/-/326/14637616/-/13r7tifz/-/index.html|title=Wisconsin Lieutenant Governor Kleefisch survives recall election|publisher=News8000.com|date=2012-06-05|access-date=2012-07-23|archive-date=January 30, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130130180853/http://www.news8000.com/news/Wisconsin-Lieutenant-Governor-Kleefisch-survives-recall-election/-/326/14637616/-/13r7tifz/-/index.html|url-status=dead}} The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] primaries took place on May 8. The recall elections were held on June 5,{{cite web|last=Hall|first=Dee J.|url=http://host.madison.com/news/local/govt-and-politics/elections/judge-oks-petition-review-extension-june-recall-election/article_67963f84-6de3-11e1-9969-0019bb2963f4.html|title=Judge OKs petition review extension, June 5 recall election|work=Wisconsin State Journal|date=March 15, 2012|access-date=March 20, 2012}} with Walker defeating Barrett. Walker was thus the first U.S. governor to continue in office after facing a recall election.[https://web.archive.org/web/20120606213327/http://nbcpolitics.msnbc.msn.com/_news/2012/06/05/12074595-walker-emerges-victorious-in-wisconsin-recall NBC], [http://www.cnn.com/2012/06/05/politics/wisconsin-recall-vote/index.html?hpt=hp_t CNN], [https://www.foxnews.com/politics// Fox News], [https://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/wire/la-wisconsin-governor-beats-recall,0,4769607.story ''Los Angeles Times''], [https://web.archive.org/web/20120606015537/http://www.cbsnews.com/8301-503544_162-57447954-503544/wisconsin-recall-walker-opens-slight-lead-as-votes-are-counted/ CBS News]. [[2012 Wisconsin Senate recall elections|Four state senate recall elections]] took place the same day as the gubernatorial recall elections, resulting in two wins by Republican incumbents, one open seat win by a Republican, and one win by a Democratic challenger, giving Democrats control of the state Senate for the remainder of the year.{{cite news|author=Stephanie Jones|url=http://www.journaltimes.com/news/local/govt-and-politics/elections/as-republicans-see-victory-wanggaard-in-razor-thin-lead-over/article_90a8c3ae-af76-11e1-ba46-0019bb2963f4.html?comment_form=true|title=Lehman declares win|publisher=Journaltimes.com|date=2012-06-05|access-date=2012-07-23}} The recall election was just the third gubernatorial recall election in U.S. history and the first one in which the incumbent was not defeated.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/06/01/us/politics/wisconsin-recall-vote-could-foretell-november-election.html |title=Recall Election Could Foretell November Vote|work=The New York Times|access-date=June 3, 2012|first=Monica|last=Davey|date=May 31, 2012}} The other recall elections were the [[1921 North Dakota gubernatorial recall election]] (which successfully recalled [[Lynn Frazier]]) and the [[2003 California gubernatorial recall election]] (which successfully recalled [[Gray Davis]]). After 2012, the [[2021 California gubernatorial recall election]] became the second recall election to fail to defeat the incumbent. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last governor election in which the Republican candidate won the counties of [[Eau Claire County, Wisconsin|Eau Claire]], [[Sauk County, Wisconsin|Sauk]], [[Green County, Wisconsin|Green]], and [[Vernon County, Wisconsin|Vernon]]. Voter turnout in the election was 57.8 percent, the highest for a gubernatorial election not on a presidential ballot in Wisconsin history up to that point.{{cite web|last=Gilbert|first=Craig|url=http://www.jsonline.com/blogs/news/160537265.html#!page=1&pageSize=10&sort=newestfirst|title=Recall turnout June 5: high in most places, insanely high in some|publisher=JSOnline|date=2012-06-27|access-date=2012-07-23}} The election was widely covered on national television. ==Background== ===Pre-certification recall campaign=== [[File:TAA Rally in the Capitol, 2012 (6879367837).jpg|thumb|Protests in the Capitol, February 14, 2012]] [[File:20111120 49 Oak Creek, Wisconsin (6399487797) (2).jpg|thumb|Recall organizers collecting petition signatures from motorists in [[Oak Creek, Wisconsin]] in November 2011]] [[File:Walker Protest Sign the Petition (6407387075).jpg|thumb|Petition signatures being collected in [[Madison, Wisconsin]] in November 2011]] Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Governor of Wisconsin|Governor]] [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]] faced a recall effort beginning in November 2011. After the contentious [[2011 Wisconsin protests|collective bargaining dispute]],[https://www.nytimes.com/2012/04/29/us/wisconsin-vote-is-first-shot-in-wider-union-war.html "Recall Election Tests Strategies for November"], April 28, 2012. Walker's disapproval ratings varied between 50 and 51% while his approval ratings varied between 47% and 49% in 2011.{{cite web|first=Patrick|last=Marley|url=http://www.jsonline.com/news/statepolitics/130173963.html|title=New poll reflects divide on bargaining limits|publisher=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel|date=September 20, 2011|access-date=January 21, 2012}}{{cite web|url=http://www.publicpolicypolling.com/main/2011/10/wisconsin-recall-prospects-dimming.html|title=Wisconsin Recall Prospects Dimming|publisher=Public Policy Polling|date=October 26, 2011|access-date=January 21, 2012}} Wisconsin law made Walker ineligible for recall until at least January 3, 2012, one year after he first took office, and the Wisconsin Democratic Party called it a "priority" to remove him from office.{{cite news|url=http://www.nbc15.com/home/headlines/Scott_Walker_Raises_25_Million_In_First_Half_Of_Year_125845278.html|title=Scott Walker Raises $2.5 Million In First Half Of Year|publisher=Nbc15.com|agency=Associated Press|date=July 19, 2011|access-date=January 21, 2012|archive-date=March 25, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120325125205/http://www.nbc15.com/home/headlines/Scott_Walker_Raises_25_Million_In_First_Half_Of_Year_125845278.html|url-status=dead}} In the first half of 2011, Walker raised more than $2,500,000 from supporters.{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2011/08/walker-recall-expected-to-proceed-061029|title=Walker recall expected to proceed|first=David|last=Catanese|publisher=Politico|date=August 10, 2011|access-date=January 21, 2012}}{{cite web|last=Stein|first=Jason|url=http://m.jsonline.com/newswatch/125889678.htm|title=Walker raises more than $2.5 million in first half of 2011|publisher=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel|date=July 20, 2011|access-date=January 21, 2012}} Walker raised $5.1 million in the second half of 2011 to battle his recall.[http://host.madison.com/wsj/news/local/govt-and-politics/with-half-the-money-coming-from-out-of-state-walker/article_72b7126c-2770-11e1-8ffb-001871e3ce6c.html "With half the money coming from out of state, Walker far outraising recall organizers"], ''Wisconsin State Journal'', December 15, 2011; retrieved December 17, 2011. In less than half of the allotted time (60 days) to collect signatures, recall organizers report collecting more than 500,000 signatures, leaving roughly one month left to collect the remaining 40,000 signatures needed to force a recall vote. On January 17, 2012, [[United Wisconsin]], the coalition that spearheaded the recall effort, along with the Democratic Party, said that one million signatures were collected, which far exceeded the 540,208 needed, and amounted to 23 percent of the state's eligible voters, 46 percent of the total votes cast in the 2010 gubernatorial election and just shy of the 1.1 million votes earned by Walker.{{cite web|url=http://gab.wi.gov/sites/default/files/percent%20results%20post%20recount_120710.pdf|title=Recount results|publisher=Wisconsin Government Accountability Board|access-date=March 20, 2012|archive-date=May 21, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120521140507/http://gab.wi.gov/sites/default/files/percent%20results%20post%20recount_120710.pdf|url-status=dead}} On January 25, 2012, a poll released by the [[Marquette University Law School]] indicated that Walker could win a recall election against potential candidates [[Tom Barrett (Wisconsin politician)|Tom Barrett]], [[Kathleen Falk]], [[David Obey]] or [[Timothy Cullen (Wisconsin politician)|Tim Cullen]].{{cite web|url=http://www.nationalreview.com/corner/289264/new-poll-delivers-scott-walker-good-news-christian-schneider|title=New Poll Delivers Scott Walker Good News|first=Christian|last=Schneider|publisher=National Review Online|date=January 25, 2012|access-date=March 20, 2012}}{{cite web|url=https://law.marquette.edu/poll/wp-content/uploads/2011/11/MLSPJanToplines.pdf|title=Marquette poll|publisher=Marquette University|access-date=March 20, 2012}} This compared to a poll released by [[Public Policy Polling]] in October 2011 that also predicted Walker would win a recall election against Barrett, Falk, [[Peter Barca]], [[Steve Kagen]] or [[Ron Kind]]. The poll also showed that more people opposed (49%) than supported (48%) the recall effort.{{cite web|url=http://www.publicpolicypolling.com/main/2011/10/wisconsin-recall-prospects-dimming.html|title=Wisconsin Recall Prospects Dimming|publisher=Public Policy Polling|access-date=October 28, 2011}} In February 2012, Walker's campaign made an additional request for more time for the petition signatures to be verified, stating that between 10 and 20% of the signatures reviewed to that point should not be counted. Democrats argued that even if 20% of the signatures were not counted there were still 300,000 more than the required number needed to initiate the recall. Democratic Party spokesman Graeme Zielinski argued Walker was just "delaying the inevitable". Additionally, in the period while signatures were being verified Barrett and Walker were able to collect unlimited campaign donations because normal campaign fundraising limits do not apply until an election is ordered.{{cite web|last=Bauer|first=Scott|title=Governor Scott Walker seeks more time for review of recall signatures|url=http://www.greenbaypressgazette.com/article/20120216/GPG0101/202160588/Governor-Scott-Walker-seeks-more-time-review-recall-signatures|publisher=greenbaypressgazette|access-date=February 17, 2012|archive-date=January 25, 2013|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130125022318/http://www.greenbaypressgazette.com/article/20120216/GPG0101/202160588/Governor-Scott-Walker-seeks-more-time-review-recall-signatures|url-status=dead}} On February 17, 2012, Dane County judge Richard Niess, who also signed the petition, denied Walker's request for additional time.{{cite news|url=http://2012.talkingpointsmemo.com/2012/02/judge-tells-walker-no-more-extensions-on-the-recall.php|title=Judge Tells Walker: No More Extensions On The Recall|first=Eric|last=Kleefeld|date=February 17, 2012|work=[[Talking Points Memo]]|access-date=March 1, 2012|archive-date=February 29, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120229201012/http://2012.talkingpointsmemo.com/2012/02/judge-tells-walker-no-more-extensions-on-the-recall.php|url-status=dead}} In March Milwaukee city officials asked Milwaukee Public Schools to contribute nearly $10 million more to the pension plan because of financial market downturns. The teachers' union, school board and the superintendent asked the legislature for the opportunity to negotiate to reduce costs.{{cite web|last1=Richards|first1=Erin|last2=Stein|first2=Jason|url=http://www.jsonline.com/news/education/union-mps-seek-talks-over-pension-hit-tu4hv8g-142409755.html|title=Union, MPS seek time to discuss contract changes|publisher=Journal Sentinel|date=March 12, 2012|access-date=March 20, 2012}} Milwaukee schools didn't take part in a 90-day window that had since closed, which allowed unions and municipal employees to make contract adjustments. The Assembly and Senate agreed to allow Milwaukee schools to reopen negotiations for compensation or fringe-benefit concessions without nullifying existing union contracts. The measure giving them 90 days passed the Assembly and Senate. Governor Scott Walker supported the measure. Other teachers' unions asked Milwaukee to withdraw its request, saying it would give Walker a political advantage in the recall election.{{cite web|url=http://www.news8000.com/news/Wisconsin-legislature-approves-Milwaukee-schools-plan/-/326/9294638/-/681ikez/-/index.html|title=Wisconsin legislature approves Milwaukee schools plan|publisher=News8000.com|date=March 14, 2012|access-date=March 20, 2012|archive-date=May 26, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130526144204/http://www.news8000.com/news/Wisconsin-legislature-approves-Milwaukee-schools-plan/-/326/9294638/-/681ikez/-/index.html|url-status=dead}} ===Certification=== On March 29, 2012, the [[Wisconsin Government Accountability Board]] released its final signature counts for the Walker recall petition. The GAB reported that 931,053 signatures were officially turned in, although the proponents had stated that approximately one million signatures were collected. Of that number, 26,114 were struck by GAB staff for various reasons and an additional 4,001 duplicates were struck. The final total certified by the GAB was 900,938 signatures.{{cite web|url=http://gab.wi.gov/node/2294|title=Recall Petition Update 11: G.A.B. Releases Final Signature Counts for Meeting Friday|publisher=Government Accountability Board|date=March 29, 2012|access-date=May 9, 2012|archive-date=May 10, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120510203804/http://gab.wi.gov/node/2294|url-status=dead}} ==Controversies== Twenty-nine circuit court judges in Wisconsin signed recall petitions against Gov. Walker, according to a [[Gannett Company|Gannett Wisconsin Media]] analysis.[http://sheboyganhub.sheboyganpress.com/article/20120318/SHE0101/203180442/29-circuit-court-judges-signed-Walker-recall-petitions 29 circuit court judges signed Walker recall petitions] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131103133716/http://sheboyganhub.sheboyganpress.com/article/20120318/SHE0101/203180442/29-circuit-court-judges-signed-Walker-recall-petitions |date=November 3, 2013 }} Among the signers was Dane County Judge David Flanagan, who was scrutinized after issuing a temporary restraining order March 6 against a Walker-backed [[voter ID]] law without disclosing his support of the recall.{{cite web|last=Rodriguez|first=Barbara|url=http://www.postcrescent.com/article/20120307/APC010401/203070547/Dane-County-Judge-David-Flanagan-temporarily-stops-new-Wisconsin-voter-ID-law|title=Dane County Judge David Flanagan temporarily stops new Wisconsin voter ID law|publisher=Postcrescent.com|date=March 7, 2012|access-date=March 20, 2012|archive-date=March 14, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120314094528/http://www.postcrescent.com/article/20120307/APC010401/203070547/Dane-County-Judge-David-Flanagan-temporarily-stops-new-Wisconsin-voter-ID-law|url-status=dead}} None of the state's sixteen appeals court judges or seven [[Wisconsin Supreme Court|Supreme Court]] justices signed the recall petition. The state Supreme Court issued an advisory opinion in 2001 saying judges are allowed to sign nominating petitions, as long as the petition language only supports putting the candidate on the ballot and does not imply an endorsement. The [[Landmark Legal Foundation]] requested an investigation to the Wisconsin Judicial Commission regarding allegations of misconduct by the judges in question.{{citation needed|date=November 2013}} It was later learned that 25 journalists at Gannett had also signed the recall petition. The newspaper group revealed the signatures in the interest of being as open as possible. Genia Lovett, representative for the organization, stated that journalists have a right to hold opinions, but must protect the credibility of their respective news organizations.{{cite news|agency=Associated Press|url=http://www.todaystmj4.com/news/local/144136885.html|title=Gannett apologizes after reporters sign Walker recall petitions|publisher=TMJ4|date=March 25, 2012|access-date=May 9, 2012|archive-date=April 27, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120427171046/http://www.todaystmj4.com/news/local/144136885.html|url-status=dead}} Other media organizations had staff who signed the recall petition.{{cite web|url=http://www.todaystmj4.com/news/local/145992565.html|title=WTMJ staffers signed Governor Walker recall petition|publisher=WTMJ|date=April 3, 2012|access-date=May 9, 2012|archive-date=May 8, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120508023853/http://www.todaystmj4.com/news/local/145992565.html|url-status=dead}} Rob Starbuck, the morning news anchor for [[Madison, Wisconsin]], television station WISC-TV, signed the Walker recall petition. The station stated that the signing was in violation of the station's policy for newsroom employees. Television stations WISN, WTMJ, WITI, WDJT and radio station WTMJ in Milwaukee discovered that some staff members signed petitions to recall Walker. Some employees at WTMJ claimed signing the recall petition was not a political act, but rather, similar to casting a vote. WTMJ stated it did not agree and indicated they would take measures to make sure their reporting was fair and balanced, and to ensure no future similar controversies. The WITI television journalist who had signed the petition was reassigned and prohibited from covering Walker-related stories.[http://www.jsonline.com/entertainment/tvradio/all-4-tv-news-operations-report-staffers-who-signed-walker-recall-petition-gg4t03l-146368405.html "News operations report that staffers signed Walker recall petition"], jsonline.com; accessed May 6, 2014.[http://www.jrn.com/tmj4/news/145992565.html "WTMJ4 report on staffers who signed Walker recall petition"], jrn.com; accessed May 6, 2014. The cost of the recall election had also drawn criticism. An estimate provided by the state Government Accountability Board showed a cost of $9 million for a statewide election. Since a primary election was also conducted for this race, Representative Robin Vos estimated the cost would be double, around $18 million.{{cite web|author=Todd Richmond Associated Press|url=http://www.journaltimes.com/news/local/breaking/survey-wis-gov-recall-will-cost-million/article_02a8d55c-38ad-11e1-bd17-0019bb2963f4.html|title=Survey: Wis. gov recall will cost $9 million: The Racine Journal Times Online|publisher=Journaltimes.com|date=January 6, 2012|access-date=June 3, 2012}} [[File:WisconsinGubernatorialPrimary2012.png|thumb|Results of the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary on May 8, 2012. Red counties had more votes for Walker than all Democrats combined. Blue counties had more votes for all Democrats combined than Walker.]] ===Costs and spending=== The recall elections were the most expensive elections in Wisconsin history.{{cite news|author=Staff|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/wisconsin-recall-unions_n_1565921|title=Wisconsin Recall Breaks Record Thanks To Outside Cash|work=Huffington Post|access-date=June 5, 2012|archive-date=June 5, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120605010217/https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2012/06/03/wisconsin-recall-unions_n_1565921.html?ref=tom-barrett|url-status=live|date=June 3, 2012}} According to the advocacy group Wisconsin Democracy Campaign, candidates and outside groups spent more than $80 million in the governor's recall race. This compares to $37.4 million spent on the 2010 Wisconsin gubernatorial election.{{cite web|last=Bauter|first=Alison|url=http://www.jsonline.com/news/statepolitics/spending-on-state-recalls-exceeds-125-million-group-says-hb5mriv-157906265.html|title=Spending on state recalls exceeds $125 million, group says|work=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel|date=June 7, 2012|access-date=June 7, 2012}} According to ''[[USA Today]]'', "More than $62 million was spent by the candidates and outside groups. Much of the $30 million raised by Walker came from outside the state. Barrett ... spent about $4 million; most of his donors live in Wisconsin."{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/politics/story/2012-06-05/wisconsin-recall-election-walker/55388788/1?csp=34news|title=Wisconsin Gov. Walker faces recall vote|publisher=USAToday.com|access-date=2012-07-23|date=June 5, 2012}} Barrett also benefited from spending by labor unions throughout the recall, estimated at another $20 million.{{Citation needed|date=February 2015}} Kathleen Falk, who was defeated by Barrett in the Democratic primary, raised about $5.2 million from public-sector unions inside and outside the state. District ! Walker ! Barrett ! Representative |- align=center ! {{party shading/Republican}}|{{ushr|Wisconsin|1|1st}} | '''57%''' | 42% | {{party shading/Republican}}|[[Paul Ryan]] |- align=center ! {{party shading/Democratic}}|{{ushr|Wisconsin|2|2nd}} | 35% | '''64%''' | {{party shading/Democratic}}|[[Tammy Baldwin]] |- align=center ! {{party shading/Republican}}|{{ushr|Wisconsin|3|3rd}} | '''52%''' | 47% | {{party shading/Democratic}}|[[Ron Kind]] |- align=center ! {{party shading/Democratic}}|{{ushr|Wisconsin|4|4th}} | 28% | '''72%''' | {{party shading/Democratic}}|[[Gwen Moore]] |- align=center ! {{party shading/Republican}}|{{ushr|Wisconsin|5|5th}} | '''68%''' | 32% | {{party shading/Republican}}|[[Jim Sensenbrenner]] |- align=center ! {{party shading/Republican}}|{{ushr|Wisconsin|6|6th}} | '''62%''' | 38% | {{party shading/Republican}}|[[Tom Petri]] |- align=center ! {{party shading/Republican}}|{{ushr|Wisconsin|7|7th}} | '''59%''' | 40% | {{party shading/Republican}}|[[Sean Duffy]] |- align=center ! {{party shading/Republican}}|{{ushr|Wisconsin|8|8th}} | '''62%''' | 38% | {{party shading/Republican}}|[[Reid Ribble]] |} ==Analysis== Despite the [[2011 Wisconsin protests|protests]], which followed shortly after Walker's inauguration, Walker's margin of victory in the recall election increased by 1 percentage point compared to the [[Wisconsin gubernatorial election, 2010|previous election]] (6.8% vs 5.8%). Approximately 350,000 more people voted in the recall election than in the 2010 election (2.5 million vs 2.15 million), making voter turnout in the recall 57.8%, the highest for a Wisconsin gubernatorial election not on a presidential ballot. The [[WOW counties|Republican bastions]] of [[Ozaukee County, Wisconsin|Ozaukee]], [[Waukesha County, Wisconsin|Waukesha]], and [[Washington County, Wisconsin|Washington]] had the highest turnouts in the state, at 74%, 72%, and 70% respectively. The Democratic bastion of [[Dane County, Wisconsin|Dane]] was not far behind, at 67% voter turnout. [[Menominee County, Wisconsin|Menominee]] had the lowest turnout in the state, with only 28% voter turnout. Walker won 60 counties in the recall election, compared to 59 in 2010. Three counties flipped from Walker to Barrett in the recall election ([[Columbia County, Wisconsin|Columbia]], [[Kenosha County, Wisconsin|Kenosha]], and [[La Crosse County, Wisconsin|La Crosse]]), while four counties flipped from Barrett to Walker in the recall election ([[Crawford County, Wisconsin|Crawford]], [[Eau Claire County, Wisconsin|Eau Claire]], [[Green County, Wisconsin|Green]], and [[Trempealeau County, Wisconsin|Trempealeau]]). Walker's margin of victory increased in 54 counties, while it decreased in 18 counties. Walker did better in most of northern Wisconsin, while Barrett did better in southeast Wisconsin and the most northern counties in the state. Twelve counties ([[Buffalo County, Wisconsin|Buffalo]], [[Calumet County, Wisconsin|Calumet]], [[Clark County, Wisconsin|Clark]], [[Door County, Wisconsin|Door]], [[Forest County, Wisconsin|Forest]], [[Kewaunee County, Wisconsin|Kewaunee]], [[Outagamie County, Wisconsin|Outagamie]], [[Pepin County, Wisconsin|Pepin]], [[Price County, Wisconsin|Price]], [[Rusk County, Wisconsin|Rusk]], [[Taylor County, Wisconsin|Taylor]], and [[Trempealeau County, Wisconsin|Trempealeau]]) had swings towards Walker by six points or more compared to the last election, while six counties ([[Columbia County, Wisconsin|Columbia]], [[Dodge County, Wisconsin|Dodge]], [[Douglas County, Wisconsin|Douglas]], [[Kenosha County, Wisconsin|Kenosha]], [[Racine County, Wisconsin|Racine]], and [[Rock County, Wisconsin|Rock]]) had swings towards Barrett by two points or more. The Democratic strongholds of [[Dane County, Wisconsin|Dane County]] and [[Milwaukee County, Wisconsin|Milwaukee County]] went more to Barrett in the recall election, while the Republican strongholds of [[Waukesha County, Wisconsin|Waukesha]], [[Ozaukee County, Wisconsin|Ozaukee]], and [[Washington County, Wisconsin|Washington]] went more Walker. Craig Gilbert of the ''[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]]'' noted the similarities between the 2010 and 2012 elections while looking at the exit poll numbers.{{cite web|last=Gilbert|first=Craig|url=http://www.jsonline.com/blogs/news/160537265.html#!page=5&pageSize=10&sort=newestfirst|title=Recall turnout June 5: high in most places, insanely high in some|publisher=Jsonline.com|date=2012-06-27|access-date=2012-07-23}} == Aftermath == ===2014 Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling=== On July 31, 2014, Scott Bauer reported for the [[Associated Press]]:
The Wisconsin Supreme Court on Thursday [July 31, 2014] upheld the 2011 law that effectively ended collective bargaining for most [Wisconsin] public workers, sparked massive protests and led to Republican Gov. Scott Walker's recall election and rise to national prominence. The 5-2 ruling upholds Walker's signature policy achievement in its entirety and is a major victory for the potential 2016 GOP presidential candidate, who is seeking re-election this year. The ruling also marks the end of the three-year legal fight over the law, which prohibits public-employee unions from collectively bargaining for anything beyond wage increases based on inflation. A federal appeals court twice upheld the law as constitutional. "No matter the limitations or 'burdens' a legislative enactment places on the collective-bargaining process, collective bargaining remains a creation of legislative grace and not constitutional obligation", Justice [[Michael Gableman]] wrote.[http://talkingpointsmemo.com/news/wisconsin-court-upholds-2011-law "2011 law which led to recall election is upheld by the Wisconsin Supreme Court, 5-2"], talkingpointsmemo.com; accessed August 19, 2014.
Chief Justice [[Shirley Abrahamson]] and Justice [[Ann Walsh Bradley]] dissented from the ruling, arguing the law unconstitutionally infringes on protected rights. ===Investigation of alleged illegal campaign coordination=== In August 2012, the first investigation, which had been launched by [[John T. Chisholm|John Chisholm]], Milwaukee County District Attorney, a Democrat, into missing funds, was rolled into a second [[Wisconsin Circuit Court#Grand jury and John Doe proceedings|John Doe probe]] based on a theory that Governor Walker's campaign had illegally coordinated with conservative groups engaged in issue advocacy during the recall elections.{{cite news|last1=Kittle|first1=MD|url=http://watchdog.org/149217/john-doe-wall-street-journal-investigation/|title='Never-ending' John Doe never ended, WSJ reports|newspaper=Wisconsin Reporter|date=June 9, 2014|access-date=April 13, 2015|archive-date=March 17, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150317041807/http://watchdog.org/149217/john-doe-wall-street-journal-investigation/|url-status=dead}} The initial John Doe judge, now retired Kenosha County Circuit Judge Barbara A. Kluka, overseeing the John Doe investigation issued 30 subpoenas and 5 search warrants. She also issued a secrecy order which meant that those being investigated were legally bound from discussing any facet of the investigation publicly.[https://www.wsj.com/news/articles/SB10001424052702304799404579155953286552832 "Wisconsin Political Speech Raid"], ''Wall Street Journal''; November 18, 2013. Shortly thereafter, she recused herself from the investigation.[http://watchdog.org/113658/judge-investigation-democrat "Judge in Democrat-led John Doe probe recuses herself"], ''Wisconsin Reporter''; October 30, 2013. Kluka's replacement, Judge [[Gregory Peterson]], quashed several subpoenas in January 2014, saying "there was no probable cause shown that they violated campaign finance laws".{{cite news|last1=Kittle|first1=MD|url=http://watchdog.org/149217/john-doe-wall-street-journal-investigation|title='Never-ending' John Doe never ended, WSJ reports|newspaper=Wisconsin Reporter|date=June 9, 2014|access-date=April 13, 2015}}[http://watchdog.org/115840/judge-milwaukee-investigation Milwaukee John Doe investigation], watchdog.org; accessed September 15, 2015. The special prosecutor{{Who|date=April 2015}} took the unusual step of filing a supervisory writ, essentially appealing Judge Peterson's decision, with the same appeals court that had denied a motion to stop the investigation.{{Cite web|url=http://watchdog.org/130571/prosecutor-john-doe-law|title=''Wisconsin Reporter'', "John Doe special prosecutor appeals judge's ruling quashing subpoenas", February 28, 2014.|accessdate=December 30, 2022|archive-date=July 26, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170726054734/http://watchdog.org/130571/prosecutor-john-doe-law/|url-status=dead}} On July 16, 2015, the Wisconsin Supreme Court closed the investigation into whether Governor Walker's campaign had illegally coordinated with outside groups by a 4–2 vote. Justice [[Michael J. Gableman]] in writing for the majority stated, "To be clear, this conclusion ends the John Doe investigation because the special prosecutor's legal theory is unsupported in either reason or law. Consequently, the investigation is closed."{{Cite news|title=Scott Walker clears big legal hurdle in Wisconsin|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-politics/wp/2015/07/16/scott-walker-clears-big-legal-hurdle-in-wisconsin/|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=2015-07-16|access-date=2015-09-15|issn=0190-8286|language=en|first1=Jose A.|last1=DelReal|first2=Jenna|last2=Johnson}} The director of [[Wisconsin Club for Growth]] (the Wisconsin arm of the national [[Club for Growth]]), [[Eric O'Keefe (political activist)|Eric O'Keefe]], defied the gag order, and filed a lawsuit alleging the probe was partisan and violated [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] rights to free expression. In a May 6, 2014 order, [[Rudolph T. Randa|Judge Rudolph T. Randa]] found the investigation had no legal basis.{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/post-politics/wp/2014/05/06/in-victory-for-walker-and-allies-federal-judge-halts-wisconsin-campaign-finance-probe|title=Judge Halts Probe|quote=The defendants are pursuing criminal charges through a secret John Doe investigation against the plaintiffs for exercising issue advocacy speech rights that on their face are not subject to the regulations or statutes the defendants seek to enforce. This legitimate exercise of O'Keefe's rights as an individual, and WCFG's rights as a 501(c)(4) corporation, to speak on the issues has been characterized by the defendants as political activity covered by Chapter 11 of the Wisconsin Statutes, rendering the plaintiffs a subcommittee of the Friends of Scott Walker and requiring that money spent on such speech be reported as an in-kind campaign contribution. This interpretation is simply wrong.|newspaper=The Washington Post|first=Rosalind S.|last=Helderman|date=May 6, 2014}} One day later, a three-judge panel ([[Diane Wood|Wood]], [[William J. Bauer|Bauer]] and [[Frank H. Easterbrook|Easterbrook]]) of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit]] in Chicago stayed Judge Randa's preliminary injunction, ruling he had overstepped his authority as prosecutors had already appealed an earlier decision in the case. Randa could issue his injunction only if he certified their appeal as frivolous. The appeals court also ruled that Judge Randa could not order prosecutors to destroy evidence collected in the five-county probe.[http://www.jsonline.com/news/statepolitics/halt-to-john-doe-probe-lifts-obstacle-to-scott-walker-re-election-bid-b99264574z1-258293621.html 7th Circuit United States Court of Appeals overturns Randa decision], jsonline.com; retrieved September 12, 2014.[http://host.madison.com/news/local/govt-and-politics/judge-s-order-tossing-john-doe-investigation-is-stayed/article_12911db4-70c9-50ac-935b-27f5f61329de.html "Judge's order tossing 'John Doe' investigation is stayed"], ''[[Wisconsin State Journal]]'', May 7, 2014; retrieved May 14, 2014.[http://watchdog.org/123377/john-doe-conservatives-wall-street-journal RE "John Doe" investigations against Republicans and conservatives in Wisconsin] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150420040026/http://watchdog.org/123377/john-doe-conservatives-wall-street-journal/ |date=April 20, 2015 }}, watchdog.org; accessed July 31, 2014.{{cite news|title=Prosecutors Allege Scott Walker At Center Of Campaign Finance Criminal Conspiracy|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/scott-walker-investigation_n_5512463|work=The Huffington Post|access-date=June 20, 2014|archive-date=June 19, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140619224018/https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/06/19/scott-walker-investigation_n_5512463.html|url-status=live|date=June 19, 2014}} Judge Randa quickly certified the appeal as frivolous and the appeals court upheld the preliminary injunction ruling that he did have the authority to issue the injunction.[http://watchdog.org/149277/court-john-doe-judge "Appeals court judge upholds judge's order shutting down John Doe probe"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150603232313/http://watchdog.org/149277/court-john-doe-judge/ |date=June 3, 2015 }}, ''Wisconsin Reporter'', June 9, 2014. At the request of the Wisconsin Club for Growth, the court unsealed documents from the investigation on June 19, 2014.{{cite news|last1=Marley|first1=Patrick|last2=Bice|first2=Daniel|last3=Glauber|first3=Bill|url=http://www.jsonline.com/news/statepolitics/john-doe-prosecutors-allege-scott-walker-at-center-of-criminal-scheme-263839791.html|title=John Doe prosecutors allege Scott Walker at center of 'criminal scheme'|newspaper=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel|date=June 19, 2014|access-date=June 19, 2014}} These documents reveal the prosecutors' theory that Governor Walker was at the center of a plan to illegally coordinate fundraising efforts with a number of outside conservative groups to help him in the 2012 recall election, bypassing state election laws. A theory that had been ruled as having no legal basis by two judges.[http://watchdog.org/143058/john-doe-judge-injunction "Judge stops WI prosecutors' John Doe probe into conservatives"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150420040029/http://watchdog.org/143058/john-doe-judge-injunction/ |date=April 20, 2015 }}, ''Wisconsin Reporter'', May 6, 2014. According to a statement by prosecutors "At the time the investigation was halted, Governor Walker was not a target of the investigation. At no time has he been served with a subpoena", and that they have "no conclusions as to whether there is sufficient evidence to charge anyone with a crime".[http://host.madison.com/wsj/news/local/govt-and-politics/scott-walker-not-a-target-john-doe-special-prosecutor-says/article_9d5579ed-039d-5f22-ac98-947469c3c22d.html "Governor Walker not a target according to 'John Doe' special prosecutor"], madison.com; accessed August 4, 2014. To date, no one has been charged in the investigation.{{cite news|title=Prosecutors allege Walker in criminal scheme regarding fundraising|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2014/06/19/scott-walker-prosecutors-criminal-probe/10891057|work=USA Today|date=June 19, 2014|access-date=November 13, 2014|first1=Fredreka|last1=Schouten|first2=Aamer|last2=Madhani}} The probe has been effectively shut down with Judge Peterson's quashing of subpoenas until the Wisconsin Supreme Court rules on whether the investigation was legal.[http://watchdog.org/187893/supreme-court-john-doe-legal "Wisconsin Supreme Court to take up John Doe complaints"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150506171635/http://watchdog.org/187893/supreme-court-john-doe-legal/ |date=May 6, 2015 }}, watchdog.org, December 17, 2014. On August 21, 2014, a number of email messages were disclosed from a previous court filing by a special prosecutor. According to ''[[Politico]]'', the emails purports to show that Walker made an early decision for money to be funneled though a group he trusted, and shows that he had a direct hand in "orchestrating the fundraising logistics of the opposition to the recalls".{{cite web|last1=Hohman|first1=James|title=The Scott Walker documents: 6 must-read passages|date=August 23, 2014 |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2014/08/the-walker-documents-6-must-read-passages-110290.html#ixzz3BH29i9QV|publisher=Politico|access-date=August 24, 2014}} According to ''[[CBS News]]'', the disclosures show that prosecutors claimed that Walker "personally solicited donations for [the] conservative group Wisconsin Club for Growth to get around campaign finance limits and disclosure requirements as he fended off the recall attempt in 2012."{{cite news|title=New emails show Scott Walker's fundraising strategy in recall election|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/new-emails-show-scott-walkers-fundraising-strategy-in-recall-election|publisher=CBS News|access-date=August 24, 2014|date=August 23, 2014}} One of the emails released read, "As the Governor discussed ... he wants all the issue advocacy efforts run through one group to ensure correct messaging. We had some past problems with multiple groups doing work on 'behalf' of Gov. Walker and it caused some issues ... The Governor is encouraging all to invest in the Wisconsin Club for Growth." ''[[The Washington Post]]'' reported that the documents released show Walker solicited donors such as [[Home Depot]] co-founder [[Ken Langone]], hedge fund manager [[Paul Singer (businessman)|Paul Singer]], and real estate businessman [[Donald Trump]] to give large contributions to a tax-exempt group that backed him during the recall efforts.{{cite news|title=Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker sought help from top GOP donors for allied group|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/wisconsin-gov-scott-walker-sought-help-from-top-gop-donors-for-allied-group/2014/08/23/aea74f38-2afd-11e4-86ca-6f03cbd15c1a_story.html|newspaper=The Washington Post|access-date=August 24, 2014|first=Matea|last=Gold|date=August 23, 2014}} Wisconsin Club for Growth reportedly only ran issues ads, none of which had to do with the recall attempt.[http://watchdog.org/174723/john-doe-eric-okeefe-investigation "Target of secret John Doe probe is fighting back and speaking out"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150317003327/http://watchdog.org/174723/john-doe-eric-okeefe-investigation/ |date=March 17, 2015 }}, ''Wisconsin Reporter'', October 2, 2014. According to a ''The Wall Street Journal'' editorial (August 24, 2014), it is "legal and common" for politicians to raise money for [[political action committee]]s, party committees, and [[501(c) organization#501(c)(4)|501(c)(4)'s]]. There are no allegations that the Wisconsin Club for Growth gave the money to Walker, or even advertised on his behalf.{{cite news|title=Hyperventilating in Wisconsin|url=https://online.wsj.com/articles/hyperventilating-in-wisconsin-over-scott-walkers-fund-raising-1408920214?_outlook|publisher=The Wall Street Journal|date=August 24, 2014}} In September 2014, lawyers asked a federal appeals court to uphold an injunction that blocks a Wisconsin prosecutor from reviving an investigation that targeted conservative organizations accused of illegally coordinating with the governor for the purpose of circumventing campaign finance limits, citing selective prosecution and violations of free speech and equal protection under the law.{{cite web|last1=Shapiro|first1=Jeffrey|title=Walker support group seeks to uphold prosecution injunction|website=[[The Washington Times]] |url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2014/sep/10/shapiro-walker-support-group-seeks-uphold-prosecut|access-date=September 12, 2014}} On September 9, 2014, the Seventh Circuit heard oral arguments on the appeal. During arguments, Judge Frank Easterbrook questioned the constitutionality of the secrecy orders, stating it's "screaming with unconstitutionality". Judge Diane Wood focused in on why the suit was filed in federal court. O'Keefe's attorneys pointed to the fact that the Wisconsin Supreme Court had yet to take up the cases filed in state court.[http://watchdog.org/169549/appeal-partisan-wisconsin/ Wisconsin prosecutors appeal for protection from blowback in partisan probe] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150506171809/http://watchdog.org/169549/appeal-partisan-wisconsin/ |date=May 6, 2015 }} Wisconsin Reporter; September 9, 2014 On September 24, 2014, the Seventh Circuit reversed Judge Randa's injunction order and dismissed the lawsuit, not based on the merits of the case, but ruling only on federal interference in a state case.[http://watchdog.org/173189/john-doe-injunction/ Appeals court reverses John Doe injunction, but Wisconsin's secret war far from over] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150506171817/http://watchdog.org/173189/john-doe-injunction/ |date=May 6, 2015 }}, ''Wisconsin Reporter'', September 24, 2014. O'Keefe filed an appeal with the U.S. Supreme Court on January 21, 2015.[http://watchdog.org/194476/suprme-court-john-doe-first-amendment O'Keefe takes his case against John Doe to U.S. Supreme Court] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150506171825/http://watchdog.org/194476/suprme-court-john-doe-first-amendment/ |date=May 6, 2015 }}, watchdog.org, January 21, 2015; accessed July 27, 2015. Wisconsin's Government Accountability Board, or GAB, performed the functions of both a state elections and ethics board during this time period and was part of the investigation due to being "presented with facts that suggested there was a violation of the law as it had been applied for years".[http://www.wpr.org/exit-interview-kevin-kennedy-executive-director-government-accountability-board "Exit Interview with Kevin Kennedy, Executive Director of the Government Accountability Board"], wpr.org, June 23, 2016 Although credited as a "model" for other states because "members are former judges chosen in a way to ensure they will not favor either major party" and "no other state has a chief election administration authority with the same degree of insulation from partisan politics"[http://www.law.uci.edu/lawreview/vol3/no3/tokaji.pdf "America's Top Model: The Wisconsin Government Accountability Board"], UC Irvine Law Review, 2013. the GAB's being part of this investigation still drew the ire of some Wisconsin Republicans. In July 2015 Governor Walker called for the dismantling of the GAB.[http://www.wkow.com/story/29587052/2015/07/20/walker-calls-for-dismantling-of-state-elections-board "Walker calls for dismantling of state elections board"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160927024628/http://www.wkow.com/story/29587052/2015/07/20/walker-calls-for-dismantling-of-state-elections-board |date=September 27, 2016 }}, wkow, July 20, 2015 The state legislature, controlled by Republicans during the 2015–16 session, passed a law doing so—which Governor Walker signed—that ended the GAB in 2016 and split its functions between boards appointed by leaders of the major political parties. In 2016, [[Salon.com]] declared that a majority of the Wisconsin Supreme Court justices who halted the investigation had been endorsed by the same conservative organizations that were being investigated. "Four of that court's seven justices were elected with $10 million in support (more than the jurists spent on their own campaigns) from Wisconsin Club for Growth and Wisconsin Manufacturers & Commerce, two of the 'independent' groups that Walker was accused of illegally coordinating with..."{{cite news |last=Fischer |first=Brendan |title=It hurts to be right: How Scott Walker proved Citizens United wrong |date=September 16, 2016 |work=Salon |url=http://www.salon.com/2016/09/16/it-hurts-to-be-right-how-scott-walker-proved-citizens-united-wrong_partner|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160917152104/http://www.salon.com/2016/09/16/it-hurts-to-be-right-how-scott-walker-proved-citizens-united-wrong_partner/|url-status=live|archive-date=September 17, 2016}} This led to some of the District Attorneys involved in the John Doe investigation appealing unsuccessfully to the [[SCOTUS|U.S. Supreme Court]].[http://host.madison.com/wsj/news/local/govt-and-politics/wisconsin-supreme-court-won-t-restart-john-doe-probe-of/article_5783e159-4447-5b10-bf54-3ad4aab69785.html "Wisconsin Supreme Court won't restart John Doe probe"], ''Wisconsin State Journal'', April 28, 2016. ''[[The Guardian]]'' reported in September 2016 that there was strong evidence of illegal coordination, based on more than 1500 pages of leaked emails.{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2016/sep/14/john-doe-files-scott-walker-corporate-cash-american-politics|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|date=September 14, 2016|title=Because Scott Walker Asked: Leaked court documents from 'John Doe investigation' in Wisconsin lay bare pervasive influence of corporate cash on modern US elections|last=Pilkington|first=Ed}}{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/19/opinion/an-email-trail-leads-to-gov-walker.html|newspaper=[[New York Times]]|date=September 19, 2016|title=An Email Trail Leads to Gov. Walker}} On October 3, 2016, the [[United States Supreme Court]] decided not to take the case despite urging by ''[[The New Yorker]]'' in order "to repair the rule of law in Wisconsin".[https://www.newyorker.com/news/news-desk/why-the-supreme-court-should-take-on-political-corruption-in-wisconsin "Why the Supreme Court Should Take On Political Corruption in Wisconsin"], newyorker.com, September 23, 2016. Political and legal scholar Howard Schweber opined that this may have been due to the US Supreme Court trying to avoid "tie outcomes".[http://www.wpr.org/listen/1001306, "US Supreme Court Declines To Hear Wisconsin's John Doe Appeal"], wpr.org, October 3, 2016. ==See also== {{Portal|Politics}} *[[2011 Wisconsin protests]] *[[2011 Wisconsin Act 10]] *[[Recall elections in Wisconsin]] *[[2012 Wisconsin lieutenant gubernatorial recall election]] *[[Wisconsin Supreme Court election, 2011]] *[[Wisconsin Senate recall elections, 2011]] *[[Wisconsin Senate recall elections, 2012]] ==References== {{reflist|colwidth=30em}} ==External links== *[http://www.iverifytherecall.com/ Database of Governor Walker and state senator recall petitions] *[http://www.jsonline.com/news/statepolitics/133164343.html Election coverage] at the ''[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]]'' **[http://www.jsonline.com/watchdog/dataondemand/140931763.html Campaign contributions interactive] {{United States general elections, 2012}} [[Category:2012 United States gubernatorial elections]] [[Category:2012 elections in Wisconsin|Gubernatorial]] [[Category:Wisconsin gubernatorial elections|2012]] [[Category:Gubernatorial recall elections in the United States|Wisconsin 2012]] [[Category:June 2012 in the United States|Wisconsin gubernatorial recall election]] [[Category:Scott Walker (politician)]]

'''Maloney''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Earl Ray Tomblin]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Earl Ray Tomblin]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsWV}} The '''2012 West Virginia gubernatorial election''' was held on November 6, 2012, to elect the governor of West Virginia. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Earl Ray Tomblin]], who was elected governor in a special election in 2011, was elected to a full four-year term. The election was a rematch of the 2011 special election. As of 2026, this was the last time a Democratic governor was re-elected in the state, the last time a Democrat won and served a full term as governor of West Virginia,{{Efn|Then-[[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Jim Justice]] won the [[2016 West Virginia gubernatorial election|2016 election]], but he became a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] in 2017.}} and the last
